abstract.text: We consider the problem of fast time-series data clustering. Building on previous work modeling the correlation-based Hamiltonian of spin variables we present an updated fast non-expensive Agglomerative Likelihood Clustering algorithm (ALC). The method replaces the optimized genetic algorithm based approach (f-SPC) with an agglomerative recursive merging framework inspired by previous work in Econophysics and Community Detection. The method is tested on noisy synthetic correlated time-series data-sets with built-in cluster structure to demonstrate that the algorithm produces meaningful non-trivial results. We apply it to time-series data-sets as large as 20,000 assets and we argue that ALC can reduce compute time costs and resource usage cost for large scale clustering for time-series applications while being serialized, and hence has no obvious parallelization requirement. The algorithm can be an effective choice for state-detection for online learning in a fast non-linear data environment because the algorithm requires no prior information about the number of clusters.

sections.summary: The paper introduces its problem, motivation, and contribution: fast unsupervised clustering for noisy, non-linear time-series, especially financial correlation matrices. It positions ALC as a serializable alternative to f-SPC that avoids arbitrary thresholding and prior cluster-number input.

source_span.end_text: As such the algorithm competes with the likes of DBSCAN [7, 20] and HDBSCAN [6, 27].

sections.summary: Introduces bootstrap resampling to mitigate correlation-matrix noise when the signal-to-noise ratio is low. It builds a filtered dependency matrix from sampled subsets, thresholds it, and extracts a final cluster configuration. Threshold 0.75 performs better than 0.5.
sections.title: Bootstrap filtering for noisy correlation matrices

source_span.end_text: ALC is 20% more robust to noise for the synthetic datasets

sections.summary: Extends ALC to nested multi-factor block correlation structures. On synthetic hierarchical systems, both ALC and HDBSCAN can recover subclusters at low noise, but HDBSCAN merges clusters or assigns noise earlier; ALC is more robust and prefers smaller, denser clusters.
sections.title: Hierarchical block correlations and robustness

sections.summary: Compares ALC to f-SPC and HDBSCAN in likelihood quality and runtime. ALC gives higher-likelihood solutions than f-SPC and scales roughly quadratically, while HDBSCAN is faster and preferable at extreme scale.
sections.title: Performance and runtime comparison

sections.summary: Concludes that ALC maximizes the Giada-Marsili likelihood by comprehensive search, is faster than Markov Chain Monte Carlo and genetic algorithms, requires no prior number of clusters, and is suitable for online state detection. It notes bootstrap cost and future work on temporal clustering, distributional assumptions, similarity measures, and implementation optimizations.
